title: Skewing for inventory
objectives: Shift quotes to reduce unwanted inventory.
Apply the rule $m = V - \gamma q$ after each trade.
Explain the cost of inventory as risk aversion times variance.

screens.prose: You make a market around a fair value of 500p, quoting 498p bid and 502p ask. Sellers have just hit your bid three times: you now hold 300 shares. If the price falls before you sell them, you lose.

state.caption: Prices in pence. You hold 300 shares.

screens.question: What should you do to your quotes?

options.why: Raising your bid invites even more sellers, so you would buy more. Raising your ask scares off the buyers you need.
Widening makes both trades rarer, including the sale you want. It does not tilt the next trade towards a sale.
Unchanged quotes leave the next trade as likely to be a purchase as a sale. You could end up holding 400 shares.

hints.text: You want the next trade to be a sale. Which of your quotes does a buyer trade with?
Buyers trade at your ask; sellers trade at your bid.
A lower ask attracts buyers. A lower bid puts sellers off. Both help you sell.

feedback.correct: A lower ask draws buyers, and a lower bid puts sellers off.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about which trade you want next, and which quote it hits.

byKey.up: You moved the quotes up. That attracts sellers and repels buyers: the opposite of what 300 extra shares need.

explain.text: Buyers take your ask, so a lower ask brings them in. Sellers take your bid, so a lower bid keeps them away. Moving both down makes your next trade more likely a sale.

screens.prose: Arrivals follow last lesson's model: traders come at $10e^{-0.5x}$ a minute to a quote $x$ pence from 500p. Your half-spread stays 2p. Slide how far both quotes move down.

derive.caption: Bid {{498 - d}}p, ask {{502 - d}}p. A sale is {{fixed(exp(d), 2)}} times as likely as a purchase: {{round(100/(1 + exp(-d)))}}% of next trades.

screens.question: Which move makes a sale about 7 times as likely as a purchase?

options.why: Moving up makes a purchase 7 times as likely. You would pile on more shares.
With no move, a sale and a purchase are equally likely.
Down 4p makes a sale about 55 times as likely, much more than 7. It also sells at 498p, below the value.

hints.text: Slide to each value and read the ratio in the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the ratio in the caption at each setting.

explain.text: Down 2p puts your ask at 500p and your bid at 496p. Buyers now meet a quote 0p away and sellers one 4p away. The ratio of rates is $e^{0.5 \times 4} = e^2 \approx 7.4$.

screens.prose: Moving both quotes together is a **skew**. A simple rule centres your quotes on $m = V - \gamma q$, where $q$ is your **inventory** in lots of 100 shares. Take $V = 500$p, $\gamma = 1$p per lot and half-spread $s = 2$p.

state.caption: Before the skew. You hold $q = +3$ lots.

screens.question: You hold $q = +3$ lots. What is your new ask, in pence?

hints.text: Find the new centre $m$ first.
The ask sits $s = 2$p above the centre.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the centre by $\gamma q$, then add the half-spread.

byKey.wrong-way: You moved the centre up by 3p. Long inventory needs the centre lower: $m = V - \gamma q$.
byKey.no-skew: That is the ask before the skew. With 3 lots long the centre drops 3p.
byKey.mid: 497p is the new centre. The ask sits 2p above it.
byKey.bid: 495p is your new bid. The question asks for the ask, 2p above the centre.

explain.text: Holding 3 lots, you centre on $500 - 3 = 497$p: bid 495p, ask 499p. Your ask is now below fair value, so buyers find you first. You give up 1p a share on the sale to cut your risk.

screens.prose: Same rule, $m = V - \gamma q$ with $\gamma = 1$p per lot and $s = 2$p. Now buyers have lifted your ask twice: you are short, $q = -2$ lots.
screens.question: What is your new bid, in pence?

hints.text: With $q$ negative, which way does $-\gamma q$ move the centre?
The bid sits 2p below the centre.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $m = V - \gamma q$ with $q = -2$, then take off $s$.

byKey.wrong-way: You moved the centre down. Short inventory needs buying, so both quotes go up: $-\gamma q = +2$.
byKey.no-skew: That is the bid before the skew. Being short 2 lots raises the centre 2p.
byKey.mid: 502p is the new centre. The bid sits 2p below it.

explain.text: Short 2 lots, you centre on $500 + 2 = 502$p: bid 500p, ask 504p. A bid at fair value draws sellers, who take you back towards flat.

screens.prose: Your risk manager caps your position at 4 lots either way. You now hold $q = +4$ lots, right at the limit. The rule puts the centre at 496p.

state.caption: The rule's quotes at $q = +4$: bid 494p, ask 498p.

screens.question: What do you quote now?

options.text: Only the ask at 498p, with no bid

options.why: One more seller at your bid takes you to 5 lots, over the limit. A bid you cannot honour must come down.
You kept the side that adds to your position and dropped the one that reduces it.
Pulling the ask removes your way back to flat. You still want buyers.

hints.text: Which trade would break the limit?
A seller hitting your bid adds a lot; a buyer at your ask removes one.
Keep the side that takes you back towards zero.

feedback.correct: At the limit you can only reduce, so only the ask stays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the quote that would push you past 4 lots.

byKey.both: One more seller at your bid takes you to 5 lots, over the limit. That bid has to come down.

explain.text: At $q = +4$ any purchase breaks the limit, so the bid comes down and only the ask stays. That is the edge case: a position limit forces a one-sided quote. At $q = 0$ the opposite holds: no skew at all.

canvas.caption: At the limit only the ask at 498p stays.

screens.prose: Two makers see the same 100 trades (seed 3). One never skews. The other uses $\gamma = 1$p per lot. When it holds $q$ lots, a sale is $e^{q}$ times as likely as a purchase.
screens.question: After trade 100 the fair value falls 5p. The maker who never skews holds 14 lots (1,400 shares). What does the fall cost it, in pounds?

hints.text: Loss = shares held × fall per share.
1,400 shares × 5p.

feedback.correct: 1,400 × 5p = 7,000p, which is £70.00. The skewing maker holds 0 lots and loses nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the shares held by the 5p fall.

byKey.lots: You multiplied the 14 lots, not the 1,400 shares. Each lot is 100 shares.
byKey.pence: That is the loss in pence. Divide by 100 for pounds.
byKey.skewed: 0 is the skewing maker's loss: it ends flat. The maker who never skews holds 14 lots.

explain.text: Without a skew, inventory is a random walk and drifts as far as 18 lots. With one, every lot held tilts the next trade back, so it never leaves 3 lots either way. Same trades, far less price risk.

screens.prose: Buyers have lifted your ask three times, so you are short, $q = -3$ lots. A colleague says: we sold, so lower our quotes to keep selling. The rule is $m = V - \gamma q$ with $\gamma = 1$p per lot, $s = 2$p.
screens.question: Where should your quotes go?

options.why: You lowered the quotes after selling. That brings more buyers and makes you shorter still, the wrong way.
You left the quotes alone. Your short of 3 lots then drifts like a random walk.
Widening both sides does not tilt the next trade towards a purchase.

hints.text: Do you need to buy or to sell to get back to zero?
Short inventory is repaired by buying, at your bid.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Short inventory needs buying, so both quotes move up.

byKey.down: You lowered the quotes after selling. That skews the wrong way: more buyers arrive and you end up shorter.

explain.text: Short 3 lots, you need sellers, so your bid rises to 501p, above fair value. Your ask rises to 505p to put buyers off. Skew against your inventory, never with it.

screens.prose: Why skew at all? Holding $q$ shares for a time $\tau$ adds variance $q^2\sigma^2\tau$ to your P&L. A maker with risk aversion $A$ dislikes variance. The Avellaneda-Stoikov model turns that into our rule, with $\tau$ the time left in the trading session: $$m = V - \gamma q, \qquad \gamma = A\sigma^2\tau$$
screens.question: The share's volatility $\sigma$ doubles. What happens to the skew per lot, $\gamma$?

options.why: You scaled $\gamma$ with $\sigma$. It scales with the variance $\sigma^2$, so doubling $\sigma$ multiplies it by 4.
You kept only the inventory in the rule. The skew per lot grows with the risk of each lot.
You moved the wrong way. More risk per lot calls for a bigger skew, not a smaller one.

hints.text: Which power of $\sigma$ appears in $\gamma$?
$\gamma = A\sigma^2\tau$, and $(2\sigma)^2 = 4\sigma^2$.

feedback.correct: $\gamma$ grows with $\sigma^2$, so it is 4 times as large.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the power of $\sigma$ in $\gamma$.

explain.text: Variance is $\sigma^2$, so twice the volatility is four times the risk per lot. A riskier share, a longer wait or a more cautious maker all mean a bigger skew. With $q = 0$ there is nothing to skew.

screens.prose: You make markets in a share's 3-month calls, quoting £2.40 bid and £2.50 ask. A fund buys 2,000 calls from you in one trade. You are now short 2,000 calls and lose if the share jumps.
screens.question: How do you move your call quotes after the trade?

options.text: Raise both, for example to £2.46 bid and £2.56 ask
Lower both, to sell more calls cheaply
options.why: You skewed with your position. Lower quotes sell even more calls and make you shorter still.
Unchanged quotes ignore a 2,000-call position. The next trade is as likely to add to it as to cut it.

options.text: Stop quoting the calls for the rest of the day
options.why: Pulling your quotes removes the bid that lets others sell calls back to you.

hints.text: You are short calls. Do you want to buy or sell calls next?
To buy calls back, others must want to sell to you at your bid.
A higher bid attracts sellers, and a higher ask stops more buyers.

feedback.correct: Short calls means you want to buy calls, so both quotes go up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out which trade takes you back towards flat.

byKey.down: You skewed with the position. Lower quotes sell more calls, the wrong way for a short.

explain.text: A short position is cut by buying, so you raise your bid to attract sellers. You raise your ask too, to deter buyers. The inventory rule from shares carries over: whatever instrument you are short, you raise both your quotes in it.

screens.prose: A morning on the desk. $V = 500$p all morning, $s = 2$p, $\gamma = 1$p per lot, and each trade is 1 lot. You start flat at bid 498p, ask 502p.
screens.question: Fill in your inventory and your quotes after each trade.

hints.text: A seller hitting your bid adds a lot; a buyer lifting your ask removes one.
After trade 1, $q = 1$, so $m = 499$p.
Each row: update $q$, set $m = 500 - q$, then bid $m - 2$ and ask $m + 2$.

feedback.correct: Your quotes follow your inventory: down as you buy, up as you sell.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Update $q$ first on each row, then centre on $m = 500 - q$.

explain.text: Inventory runs 1, 2, 1, 0, −1. The centre runs 499, 498, 499, 500, 501p, and each quote sits 2p either side. After trade 5 you are short, so your bid of 499p tempts sellers back.

screens.prose: At 16:20 you hold 20 lots, 2,000 shares of a £5.00 share. Your desk cuts such positions to zero before the 16:30 close, even at a small loss. Suppose the price can gap 2% overnight before you can trade again.
screens.question: Why does the desk go flat before the close?

options.text: Overnight they cannot trade, so the position carries a large variance, $q^2\sigma^2\tau$, and earns no spread
Exchanges require every position to be closed each day
options.why: No such rule exists for shares. The desk chooses to go flat because of the risk.
You assumed a direction. Overnight moves go both ways; the problem is their size, not their sign.

options.text: Holding shares overnight costs a fee
options.why: You looked for a charge. The real cost is risk: a 2% gap on £10,000 is about £200 either way.

hints.text: What can you do with the position between 16:30 and 08:00?
Nothing: no trades, so no spread and no way to cut it.
The variance is $q^2\sigma^2\tau$, and overnight $\sigma^2\tau$ is large.

feedback.correct: A long, untradeable wait means large variance for no spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about risk you cannot trade out of.

explain.text: A 2% gap on 2,000 shares at £5.00 is about £200, up or down, with no spread to earn meanwhile. Counting the night in $\tau$, the skew rule agrees: $\gamma$ is large, so you shed inventory hard into the close. In the model itself $\tau$ stops at the close, so its skew fades as the close nears.

ideas: Inventory is price risk: after buying, move both quotes down; after selling, move both up.
Centre on $m = V - \gamma q$; a skewed maker's inventory keeps returning to zero instead of wandering.
The skew per lot is $\gamma = A\sigma^2\tau$; at $q = 0$ there is no skew, and at a position limit only one side stays.
summary.trap: Skew against your inventory, never with it: after selling, quotes go up. And never hold a position hoping for a rebound.

quiz.question: What is your ask, in pence?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $m = V - \gamma q$, then add $s$.

byKey.wrong-way: You moved the centre up. Long inventory moves it down.
byKey.no-skew: You left out the skew of $\gamma q = 4$p.
byKey.gamma1: You moved the centre by $q$ alone. Each lot moves it $\gamma = 2$p.

quiz.prose: $V = 500$p, $s = 2$p, $\gamma = 1$p per lot. You hold no shares.
quiz.question: What are your bid and ask?

options.why: You skewed as if you held a lot. With $q = 0$ the skew $\gamma q$ is zero.
You used 1p either side. The half-spread is still 2p.

feedback.correct: With no inventory there is no skew.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $\gamma q$ with $q = 0$.

explain.text: $q = 0$ gives $m = V = 500$p, so you quote 498p and 502p. The skew only appears once you hold something.

quiz.prose: You hold 6 lots bought at 498p. News moves fair value to 490p. A colleague says: hold them and keep the old quotes until the price comes back.
quiz.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: Fair value already includes the news, so waiting adds risk with no expected gain; quote around 490p and skew down
Nothing: prices always return to where you bought
options.why: You treated your purchase price as an anchor. The market does not know what you paid.

options.text: You should buy more at 490p to average down
options.why: Buying more raises the position you are already worried about. Skew lowers it.

feedback.correct: Your cost is history; the risk is today's.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what fair value says, not what you paid.

explain.text: At a fair value of 490p a rebound is no more likely than a further fall. Holding 6 lots only keeps the variance. Re-centre on 490p and skew: $m = 490 - 6\gamma$.

quiz.prose: A maker uses $\gamma = A\sigma^2\tau$. It moves from a share with daily volatility 1% to one with 3%, all else equal.
quiz.question: By what factor does its skew per lot change?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The skew scales with the variance, $\sigma^2$.

byKey.three: You scaled with $\sigma$. The skew scales with $\sigma^2$, so 3 times the volatility is 9 times the skew.

explain.text: Variance goes from $1^2$ to $3^2$, a factor of 9, and $\gamma$ follows it.
